translations.text: Of our holy father Basil, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia: encomium of the holy Forty Martyrs.

When could one who is a friend of the martyrs ever have enough of remembering them? For the honor that the other, lesser servants show to the king's own beloved servants is a sign of their loyalty toward their lord. And this too is evident,
that whoever calls those courageous men blessed and praises them will not fall short of imitating them in similar times. So call the martyrs blessed with sincerity,
so that you too may become a martyr in intention and attain the worthiness of their same reward without persecution, without fire, without torments.
But the praise now set before us is not of one person only, nor of two, nor does the number of those blessed ones reach only as far as ten; rather, they are forty men, whom,
as though they had one soul in those many bodies, thus with one mind and a union of faith showed one endurance in tortures and one battle against the lawless for the sake of godliness.
All are close to one another, equal in mind and equal in struggle; therefore they also became equally worthy of those crowns of righteousness.
What speech, then, could worthily attain to their praise? Not even if there were forty tongues would they be able to glorify fittingly the virtue of so many men.
For even if the one we were praising were only one, it would be enough to overcome the power of our speech, let alone so great a multitude,
that camp of valiant soldiery, that battle array, impossible to overcome, unconquered even in battles and beyond the reach of praise.
Come then, let us bring them into our midst by remembrance, set before those gathered here the benefit that comes from them, and display their virtues and valiant deeds as if by depicting them.

For historians and painters also often display victories in battles: the former adorn them with words, and the latter depict them with pigments, and in this way both of them rouse many to emulate those deeds,
for what speech displays to the hearing, the image proclaims silently through its likeness.

In the same way, let us call to the memory of all the courage of these blessed ones and set their deeds before their sight, so that we may thus rouse to emulate them souls that are valiant and akin to them in mind. For this is the encomium of martyrs: the moving of those gathered toward virtue.

for the deeds of the saints do not allow themselves to be subjected to the rules of rhetorical embellishment, since whoever praises someone draws the force and the terms of his praise from worldly words,

But as for those to whom the world is crucified, and they to the world, how could the world offer on their behalf words of praise of its own? Those saints did not have one homeland, for one was from one country and another from another. Shall we then call them people without a city,
or citizens of the whole world? For just as, when money is contributed to a common fund, what is contributed by each becomes common to all,
so too the homeland of each of these blessed ones is common to all, and all are from everywhere, for they give to one another the lands from which they came.
And besides, why is it necessary to speak of their country? It is right rather that we inquire what their city is now. The city of the martyrs, then, is that city of God,
whose craftsman and builder is God: the heavenly Jerusalem, the free city, a stranger to slavery, the mother of Paul and of those like him.
Their human kindred differed from one to another, but spiritually all had one kindred,

for God is the common Father of them all, and all are brothers of one another, not born of one father and mother, but joined to one another by the adoption of the Holy Spirit and by the unity of love.

A holy assembly, a great addition to the holy ones who have glorified the Lord from all ages, who did not gather there one by one, but all arrived together in a single moment. And what the manner of their departure from here was, listen.
These men, through bodily valor, beauty of youth and strength of might, became distinguished among the many peoples, and for this reason
they were enrolled in the army, and for the valor of their fighting, their fearlessness and their courage they received much honor from the kings and were renowned among all.

Then that godless and lawless proclamation was proclaimed: to deny Christ, or else to fall into many tortures. All kinds of tortures were being brought on, and great was the wrath of those judges of falsehood against the servants of God. Plots and evil deaths were coming upon them, tortures of every sort were being devised, and the torturers stood ready: blazing fire, and sharpened sword, and raised stake, pits dug out, cartwheels prepared, and all those evils.
Then some fled, and some bowed to that lawlessness, and some trembled and hid, and some, before tasting the tortures, took fright merely from hearing of them.

Others, when they came near those torments, were defeated, and others again entered the contest but could not endure the torments to the end, and merely partway through their contest they grew weary, and,
like those tossed by storms at sea, they sank and lost even the cargo of endurance that they had.
Then these invincible soldiers of Christ came forward into the midst, when the governor was displaying the king's letter and demanding obedience to its words.
But they, with fearless hearts, bravely trusting in Christ, were not frightened at all by those tortures, but confessed themselves Christians.

O blessed tongues, which uttered that blessed cry! The air received it and was made holy; the angels heard it and clapped their hands with joy; the devil with his servants was wounded; and the Lord recorded it in the heavens.
Each one, then, coming forward into the midst, said, "I am a Christian." And just as at the enrollment of soldiers,
those who are entering into battle state their names and immediately go over to the soldiers already enrolled and stand with them,
so these men then abandoned the names given them from birth, and each called himself by the name of the Savior of all.
And all did likewise: the second followed the first,
…to the point that the name of all became one, for no one was any longer called this or that, but all were named Christian.
What then did that tyrant do, crafty and wicked as he was? He tried to seduce them, sometimes with soft words and sometimes with harsh ones.
He first began to speak to them with cunning, so that in this way he might undo the strength of their piety, and he said to them:
"Do not give your youth over to torture, do not bring an untimely death upon yourselves in exchange for this sweet life,

"for it is a wicked thing that you, who shone forth courageously in battles, should perish by the death of evildoers." On top of all this he held out wealth and goods to them, set before them honor from the kings, promised them a multitude of gifts, and with countless devices strove to bend them.

But when they would not give way to apostasy from their resolve and from their confession of Christ, he then turned to the other kind of device and threatened them with wounds and death and a countless multitude of torments. Such were the tyrant's words; but hear also the martyrs' words, what they said to him:
"Why do you try to seduce us, O fighter against God, into departing from the living God and serving foul demons, and promise us those good things of yours?
What will you give us as great as what you take away from us? We hate gifts, which lead the way to loss; we do not accept honor, the mother of insult and dishonor.
"For you give us goods that remain here, glory that withers; you make us beloved of a mortal king, but you estrange us from the true King. Why do you so meanly promise us a little pleasure?
The whole world together with its delights is despised by us; these visible good things are not worth the hope of those good things that we long for.
"Do you see this heaven, how beautiful it is to behold, and how great? And what the earth is like? And the wonders made in it?
Not one of these is equal to the blessedness of the righteous, for all this passes away, but what is ours endures.
We long for one gift, which is the crown of righteousness; we are captivated by love for one glory, which is found in the kingdom of heaven; we are lovers of honor, of that heavenly honor.
We fear one torment, which is Gehenna; that fire is terrible to us. But this fire kindled by you is our servant, for it knows how to draw back from the bodies of martyrs.
We count your wounds as children's arrows,
for you torture the flesh, which, if it proves able to endure much, will be crowned more brilliantly, and if it dies soon,
will depart, having escaped from judges so savage. You who have received lordship over bodies, and contend to obtain power over souls as well,
you who, if you are not honored by us more than our God, grow enraged as though grievously insulted by us, and bring those terrible tortures upon us,
against whom you can show no other charge than piety. But do not be deceived, for you have not met with the fearful and the weak and those who love this passing life.

for, for the love of God, behold, we are ready to be cut apart limb by limb, to be bound on the wheels of a cart, to be given over to fire, and to accept every torment. For all this will be exchanged for us before the Lord: instead of the beating of the flesh, a garment of light will shine upon us at the resurrection; instead of dishonor, a crown; instead of prison, the kingdom; and instead of condemnation with the lawless, being with the angels. Sow much in us, so that we may reap still more."

But when that arrogant barbarian heard such words, he could not endure the boldness of those valiant men, but boiled with anger and sought a means by which he might find a way to bring a bitter and long death upon them. And so he found a means, and understand how wicked it was.
For he saw the nature of that land, how cold it was, and the season of the year, for it was winter, and he waited for the night,

when the severity of the frost had increased, for the north wind, which is called Boreas, was blowing fiercely that night. Then he ordered that they be stripped and made to stand on the ice of the lake all night, so that in this way they would perish.
But you who have experienced cold surely know how unbearable this form of torment is.
For it is not even possible for others to understand it well, except those who know the nature of the thing from experience.

For bodies that have fallen into harsh cold first turn livid, when the blood thickens from the ice; then they are seared and shattered, for the teeth strike against one another, the joints come loose, and the whole body is in anguish.
And there is bitter pain and inexpressible agony, which reaches the brain, and the taste of that evil is bitter.

Then the extremities of the body drop off and are seared as if by fire. For the blood flees from the extremities of the body and takes refuge in the depths of the body; and the places it departs from it leaves dead, while wherever it arrives it multiplies the pain, as death comes on little by little through that thickening of the blood.

So then they were condemned to be under the open air, at a time when the lake in which the contest of the saints took place was like a plain, a racecourse for horses, through its transformation by the ice; it had been made firm by the frost and was a path that feet could walk without stumbling. And the rivers, which used to flow ceaselessly, were then bound by ice and had stopped their flowing. The soft nature of water had been changed into the hardness of stone, and the fierce howlings of the north wind brought death upon all who were outdoors.

Then they heard that command of the ruler, and understand at this point the invincibility of those men: for with joy each one threw off even his last garment, and thus they rushed to that death by frost as if to the seizing of spoils. In this way they urged on and strengthened one another, saying:
"It is not a garment, brothers, that we are stripping off, but we are casting away the old man, who is corrupted by the desires of deception.
We thank you, Lord, for together with this garment we are being stripped of sin.

"O young men, let us strip off for Christ's sake this garment which we put on through the serpent; let us not spare these perishable garments for the sake of the paradise which we lost. 'What shall we render to the Lord?' For our Lord too was stripped naked.
What great thing is it for a servant if he suffers like his master, or even more? The Lord himself, we are [?],
which we have put off. For that boldness belongs to the soldiers: they stripped it off and divided the clothing. Now therefore let us blot out, by our own selves, the written accusation against us.
"Bitter is this winter, but sweet is paradise. Painful is this frost, but desirable is that rest of the righteous.
"Let us be patient a little longer, and the bosom of the patriarch Abraham will give us rest. With this one night let us purchase all the ages:
"let us allow our feet to be burned, so that we may walk with the angels forever; let us allow our hands to drop off, so that they may have boldness to be raised up to the King.
"How many soldiers among us have died in battle to prove themselves to that transient king,
"and shall we not give this life for the true King?
"How many evildoers have undergone death for their lawlessness, and shall we not endure death for righteousness?

"Let us not give way, O comrades and soldiers; let us not turn our backs to the devil, but let us fight him face to face. Let us not give ground to that enemy, for these bodies of ours are corruptible flesh, and let us not spare them. Since death is certainly with us, let us die now, so that we may live.
"Let this sacrifice of ours be before you, O Lord, and may we be offered up as a living burnt offering, pleasing to you, burned by this frost. Good is this sacrifice, for this burnt offering is new,
which is burned not by fire but by cold." With such words of comfort they spoke to one another and strengthened one another, as though they had been posted as guards in the warfare of the army,
so they passed that night, bravely enduring those transient hardships, rejoicing in the hope of the good things to come, laughing and mocking the devil.
And there was only one prayer among them all: "Forty we entered this contest; may all forty be crowned. O King, let not even one be missing from this number. Honorable is the number
which you honored with the fast of forty days,
through which the Law came into the world; for forty days Elijah fasted, and he saw the Lord."
Such was their prayer. But one of their number grew weary of those sufferings and, losing heart, fled, and he left countless grief to those saints.
Yet the Lord did not allow their prayers to prove in vain.

For the man to whom the guarding of the martyrs had been entrusted had set up his resting place nearby and was watching them to see what the outcome would be, and he was ready to receive in the bath those soldiers who fled.
For they had devised this stratagem too, that their contest should be near the bath, which offered swift help to those who turned back.

And just as those lawless men cunningly contrived this stratagem, so that the place of their suffering should be such that the ready availability of comfort would loosen their resolve and draw it to itself,
But the expedient they devised in this way only made the endurance of the martyrs shine forth all the more brilliantly.

For the one who endures is not the person who can find no consolation and remains in affliction against his will; rather, the truly enduring person is the one who has relief freely available and yet goes on enduring in his afflictions.

And as those blessed ones were struggling and the guard was watching for the end, he then saw a strange vision: powers come down from heaven, distributing great gifts to those soldiers as though from a king.

And they gave those gifts to all the others, but they left one alone uncrowned, for they did not deem him worthy of the heavenly honor, since he had thus become faint-hearted in those pains and had gone over to the adversaries.
Alas, a pitiable thing for the righteous to behold: the soldier a fugitive, the warrior taken captive, the sheep of Christ snatched away by wild beasts. And this is the most pitiable thing of all,

that he fell away from the heavenly life and did not attain even the life of this world; for as soon as he came near the heat, immediately his flesh was dissolved and melted away, and that lover of the flesh fell, having become a transgressor in vain.
And when the guard saw him fleeing and going into the bath, he set himself in the place of that faint-hearted one:
he threw off his clothing, joined himself to those naked men, and cried out with the saints the same cry: "I am a Christian."

And in an instant, by this change of his, he astonished those who were there, completed the number, and consoled the grief they felt over the fugitive. He was like soldiers drawn up in battle array, who, when one of the foremost shield-bearers falls, immediately fill up the rank, so that their unity may not be broken by that gap. So this man did: he saw those heavenly wonders, recognized the truth, attached himself to the King,
was numbered with the martyrs, and renewed the event of the apostles: Judas went out and Matthias came in.
He became like Paul, who yesterday was a persecutor and today became a preacher.

He too received his calling from heaven; "not from men, nor through men" did he believe in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. He was baptized in his name, not by another but by his own faith, not with water only but with his own blood.

And so, when day dawned, while they were still alive, they were given over, broken as they were, to the fire, and the remains left by the fire were cast into the river. And thus the contest of these blessed ones encompassed all the created elements:
on earth they contended, under the air they were tormented, to the fire they were given, and the water received them.

Theirs is the saying: "We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into a place of rest." These are the ones who stand around this land of ours like strong towers and give us security from our adversaries.
And they have not confined themselves to one place, but have made their dwelling in many villages and cities and have adorned many lands.
And this is the wonder: they do not go to give help separated one by one, but move about united.
O this wonder! Their number is neither diminished, nor does it admit of any increase.

If you divide them into a hundred, they do not go beyond their number; if you gather them into one, even so they are all forty. Like the nature of fire, which reaches in its entirety to the one who kindles from it, and again is wholly present with the one
who has it, so also the forty are all together, and all of them are with each one.

O ungrudging good, inexhaustible grace, ready help of Christians, assembly of martyrs, camp of the victorious, company of those who glorify the Lord! How much labor would you have undertaken to find even one
who would be an intercessor for you before the Lord? Behold, here are forty who together offer prayer to God.
Where two or three are gathered in the name of the Lord, there the Lord is among them; but where forty such men are, what doubt could there be that the Lord dwells among them?
Let the one in distress flee to the forty, and let the one who rejoices go to them as well: the former to find release from his distress, the latter that his good fortune may be preserved.
Here let the God-fearing woman come, praying for her children, and she who asks for the return of a husband who has gone away, or for the life of one who has fallen sick.
Let your prayer be to these martyrs. Young men, imitate these who are your own age. Fathers, pray to be the father of such sons. Mothers, hear the deed of that good mother!

The mother of one of these blessed ones saw that the others had been finished off by the ice and the crushing, but that her own son was still alive because of his courage and his great endurance of suffering, and

that the tormentors had left him, as one who could still be turned over to their side. Then that courageous mother, like Abraham offering his sacrifice, took up her son with her own hand and laid him on the cart on which the others had been loaded and were going to the fire. Truly she was the mother of a martyr,
for she did not shed tears of the kind that show weakness, nor did she speak any word improper and unworthy of that moment, but she said to him:

"Go, my child, on that good road that leads to life, with those who are your own age, with those your companions. Do not be missing from that camp. I will not accept that you should stand before Christ the King after the others, for it seemed to me like death when I saw you left behind. For I see the crowns that are to be given to them, and my heart is pressed with anguish if you too do not attain them. But come, O blessed one, and meet your end with the others, so that I may boast that I brought forth a courageous martyr from my womb. Endure patiently a little longer and you have conquered; a little longer and I shall be blessed, for I shall be called the mother of so courageous a martyr. Of this alone I am afraid: that you may be left behind." Truly,
he was a good shoot of that good root. That courageous mother showed that he had been raised by the teaching of godliness even more than by milk.
And having been raised in this way, he was sent off in this way by that good mother, and the devil went away ashamed,

For he stirred up all created things against them, and he found all of them conquered by the virtue of those blessed ones: the night, full of ice and frost; the cold earth; that season of the year, winter; the nakedness of their bodies.
O holy camp, O honored company, O undivided unity, O common guardians of the human race, good helpers in distress,
offerers of prayers, mighty intercessors, valiant in battle, towers of piety, brave ones, victors in the contest and fearless in mind, stars of the world, flowers of the churches,
it was not the earth that covered you, but the heavens received you, and the gates of paradise were opened to you.
O wondrous deed, worthy to be beheld by the host of angels, worthy of the patriarchs, the prophets, the apostles and the righteous!

Men who in the time of their youth so despised this world and life, who loved God more than parents and more than children, who, while still at the age of their joy, spurned this passing life, who glorified God in their members, became something to be pointed at by the finger before the world and angels and men.
They raised up the fallen, they strengthened the wavering, the desire and zeal of the pious

they multiplied. They raised up one equal victory of the fear of God and of right belief for all of them, and they were adorned with an equal crown of righteousness by Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and might, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
